slides.title: Chapter 8: Digital Signatures
slides.sub: What a signature proves and commits to, how Schnorr and ECDSA work, and what moved since print

items.body: Picture: the Bitcoin logo, public domain (Wikimedia Commons). Python 3.14.6; Bitcoin Core 31.1.0 results are recorded, not run here.

slides.notes: This deck explains how a Bitcoin signature works and what it commits to. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library. Bitcoin Core 31.1.0 was run once on a test network, and its answers are only read back.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.sub: Seven parts; every number is a slide you can jump to

items.label: 8. Since the book went to print
code examples with a picture of each result

slides.notes: The route has seven parts that follow the order of the chapter. Three true stories and twenty code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.take: Seven parts, twenty examples, three true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

items: What must a verifier have before it can answer yes or no?
What does each SIGHASH flag commit to, and what does SINGLE do with no matching output?
How does a three-move proof become a 64-byte Schnorr signature?
Why are keys that simply add up unsafe, and what does MuSig2 change?
Why can an ECDSA signature take two forms, and what do consensus and policy each accept?
Why does a repeated nonce leak the key, and what does RFC 6979 do about it?
What did segregated witness change in what is signed?

slides.notes: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.

slides.title: Foundations of digital signatures
slides.sub: A signature is a wax seal that only the owner of the ring can press.

items.meaning: Three inputs go in and a yes or no comes out.
items.analogy: Think of a bank clerk who checks cheque, ID and signature card.

items.meaning: Two moduli: scalars wrap at n, coordinates at p.
items.analogy: Think of two clocks of different sizes on one wall.

items.meaning: What is signed is a digest of the transaction.
items.analogy: Think of signing the fingerprint of a contract, not the paper.

slides.notes: A digital signature is a proof that the holder of a private key approved a message. This part shows what verification needs, why two moduli appear, and what is really signed.

slides.title: Foundations of digital signatures (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Digital Signatures
items.meaning: Proof that the owner of a private key approved a message.
items.analogy: Think of a handwritten signature that nobody else can forge.

items.label: How Digital Signatures Work
items.meaning: A signer holds a secret; everyone checks with the public key.
items.analogy: Think of a padlock anyone can close but only you can open.

items.label: Creating a Digital Signature
items.meaning: The signer combines the message digest, the secret key and a nonce.
items.analogy: Think of pressing a personal seal into hot wax.

slides.notes: These cards cover Digital Signatures, How Digital Signatures Work and Creating a Digital Signature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Three inputs, one answer
slides.sub: Verifying an ECDSA signature with the chapter's library

groups.note: A secret key signs a message; the public key is what others hold.
Two altered inputs: a flipped bit in the message, and another key.

rows: v = lambda p, m: L.ecdsa_verify(p, m, sig)
checks = [v(pk, msg), v(pk, bad), v(other, msg)]
groups.note: Only the true triple is accepted; every change gives False.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: four inputs, one verdict each
The signature is 70 bytes long. Only the unchanged triple of message, key and signature is accepted.

slides.notes: Verification takes a message, a public key and a signature, and answers yes or no. We flip one bit of the message, then swap the key, and both attempts fail. Only the true triple passes. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Change the message, the key or the signature and the answer turns to False

slides.title: Foundations of digital signatures (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Verifying the Signature
items.meaning: Message, public key and signature go in; yes or no comes out.
items.analogy: Think of a clerk comparing your signature with the card on file.

items.label: discrete logarithm problem
items.meaning: Given a point, finding the number that produced it is infeasible.
items.analogy: Think of mixing paint: easy to mix, impossible to unmix.

slides.notes: These cards cover Verifying the Signature and discrete logarithm problem. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Scalars wrap at n, coordinates at p
slides.sub: Two moduli, two clocks of different sizes

groups.note: A remainder keeps a number inside a fixed range, like the hours of a clock.
The response s is reduced twice, once modulo n and once modulo p, and checked.
The group order n and the field prime p are different 256-bit numbers.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: does sG = kG + eX hold?
The two primes differ by a number of 129 bits, so n and p are different clocks.

slides.notes: The signature equation lives in the group of curve points, whose order is n. Reducing the response modulo n makes the equation hold, reducing it modulo p does not. The two numbers differ by 129 bits. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The book says everything is modulo p; the response is reduced modulo n

slides.title: What is signed is a digest
slides.sub: A single satoshi changes the whole digest

groups.note: Two identical transactions of two inputs and two outputs.
In the second one, a single output amount is raised by one satoshi.
The digest is what gets signed; any change of the covered bytes changes it.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the digest that is signed
The same bytes give the same digest. One satoshi more gives a different one, and the old signature no longer fits.

slides.notes: A signature is made over a hash of selected transaction fields. The same transaction gives the same digest, and raising one output by a satoshi gives a completely different one, so the signature no longer fits. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The signature covers a hash of the transaction, not the bytes themselves

slides.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH)
slides.sub: A flag chooses how much of the letter the seal covers.

items.meaning: A flag is one byte appended to the signature.
items.analogy: Think of a tick box printed at the bottom of a form.

items.meaning: Each flag fixes some fields and leaves others open.
items.analogy: Think of a contract with some clauses left blank.

items.meaning: SINGLE with no matching output signs the number one.
items.analogy: Think of a lock that opens when the keyhole is missing.

slides.notes: A signature need not cover the whole transaction. One byte, the SIGHASH flag, chooses what it covers. We measure what each flag commits to and meet the bug of SINGLE.

slides.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH) (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Signature Hash Types (SIGHASH)
items.meaning: One byte says which parts of the transaction the signature covers.
items.analogy: Think of a tick box that says how much of the contract you sign.

items.label: signature hash
items.meaning: The digest of the transaction fields that is actually signed.
items.analogy: Think of the fingerprint of a document.

items.label: SIGHASH_ALL
items.meaning: Signs all inputs and all outputs; the default.
items.analogy: Think of signing a cheque with payee, amount and date all filled in.

items.label: SIGHASH_NONE
items.meaning: Signs the inputs but no output.
items.analogy: Think of a signed blank cheque.

slides.notes: These cards cover Signature Hash Types (SIGHASH), signature hash, SIGHASH_ALL and SIGHASH_NONE. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A flag is one byte
slides.sub: Three base values and one modifier bit

groups.note: Bitcoin knows three base flags and one modifier, each a small number.

rows: combos = [b | acp for b in base]
groups.note: The modifier is a single high bit, so it combines with any base flag.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: flag values (ACP = ANYONECANPAY)
ANYONECANPAY is 128, the top bit, so adding it to a base flag gives 129, 130, 131.

slides.notes: The flag appended to a signature is a single byte. The three base flags are 1, 2 and 3. The modifier ANYONECANPAY is 128, the top bit, which is why it can be added to any base flag. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: ANYONECANPAY is the top bit, so it combines with every base flag

slides.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH) (2 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: SIGHASH_SINGLE
items.meaning: Signs only the output with the same number as the input.
items.analogy: Think of initialling a single line of an invoice.

items.label: SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY
items.meaning: Signs only this input; others may add theirs.
items.analogy: Think of a collection tin that anyone may add to.

items.label: BIP118
items.meaning: A proposal for signatures that leave out the coin they spend.
items.analogy: Think of a ticket valid for any seat in the row.

items.label: SIGHASH_DEFAULT
items.meaning: Taproot's zero byte, which means the same as ALL and is left out.
items.analogy: Think of the standard setting you never have to tick.

slides.notes: These cards cover SIGHASH_SINGLE, SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY, BIP118 and SIGHASH_DEFAULT. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: What each flag commits to
slides.sub: Change one field and see whether the hash moves

groups.note: Six flag values: the three base flags, alone and with the modifier.

rows: cm = {f: C.sighash_commitments(f) for f in flags}
groups.note: For each flag, change one field at a time and see whether the hash moves.

rows: count = {hex(f): sum(cm[f].values()) for f in flags}
groups.note: Count the fields that each flag covers, out of the five that were probed.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: fields covered, of the 5 probed
ALL covers 5 of 5 fields, NONE with ANYONECANPAY only 1: the field pattern is ....Y.

slides.notes: We change one field of the transaction at a time and ask if the digest moves. ALL covers all five probed fields. The other flags leave some open, which is what lets others complete a transaction. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Only plain ALL covers every probed field, other inputs' sequences included

slides.title: SINGLE with no matching output
slides.sub: The bug the book does not mention

groups.note: A transaction with three inputs but only one output.

rows: d = lambda i: L.sighash_legacy(b'\x51', tx, i, 3).hex()
groups.note: SINGLE signs the output with the same number as the input being signed.
Inputs one and two have no output: the digest is the number one.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: signature hash of each input
Inputs 1 and 2 have no output of their own, so the legacy algorithm signs the constant one.

slides.notes: SIGHASH_SINGLE signs the output with the same number as the input. For inputs one and two there is none, so the legacy algorithm signs the constant one, which holds for any transaction. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: A digest equal to the number one can be reused on any transaction

slides.title: Schnorr signatures
slides.sub: Schnorr is a seal whose imprints can be added together.

items.meaning: A three-move proof becomes a signature by hashing.
items.analogy: Think of a quiz whose questions are drawn by a dice you cannot cheat.

items.meaning: Fixed sizes, x-only keys and tagged hashes.
items.analogy: Think of a standard envelope that fits every letterbox.

items.meaning: Keys and signatures add up, with one trap.
items.analogy: Think of pooling several keys into one master key.

items.meaning: Any two of three key holders can sign.
items.analogy: Think of a vault that opens when two of three managers turn their keys.

slides.notes: Schnorr signatures began as a proof of identity. We turn the proof into a signature, meet the BIP340 format, and see why keys that add up bring both multisignatures and a trap.

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (1 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Schnorr Signatures
items.meaning: A signature s = k + e x, proven by one equation on points.
items.analogy: Think of a seal whose imprints can be added.

items.label: Serialization of Schnorr Signatures
items.meaning: A BIP340 signature is 64 bytes: R's x coordinate and s.
items.analogy: Think of a form with two fixed boxes.

items.label: Schnorr-based Scriptless Multisignatures
items.meaning: Several signers produce one ordinary signature.
items.analogy: Think of a group photo that looks like a single portrait.

items.label: Schnorr-based Scriptless Threshold Signatures
items.meaning: A subset of the key holders produces one ordinary signature.
items.analogy: Think of a committee vote that leaves one signature on the minutes.

slides.notes: These cards cover Schnorr Signatures, Serialization of Schnorr Signatures, Schnorr-based Scriptless Multisignatures and Schnorr-based Scriptless Threshold Signatures. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The protocol with whole numbers
slides.sub: Why the book first explains Schnorr with integers

groups.note: Secret x, nonce k and challenge e; the 'point' of a number is just 5 times it.
The response s mixes nonce and secret; the check sG = kG + e xG holds.
With plain integers anyone can divide and read the secret: that is why points are used.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: one round with whole numbers
The proof holds, but dividing xG by G returns the secret 3: with points that division is impossible.

slides.notes: The book teaches the protocol with whole numbers first. The proof works: s times G equals the commitment plus the challenge times the public key. But dividing the public key by G reveals the secret. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: With plain integers anyone divides and reads the secret; points forbid that

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (2 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: challenge
items.meaning: The value e that ties the nonce point to the message.
items.analogy: Think of a question the exam board sets after you commit to an answer.

items.label: Fiat-Shamir transform
items.meaning: Replace the verifier's random challenge by a hash.
items.analogy: Think of letting a dice-rolling machine play the examiner.

items.label: BIP340
items.meaning: The specification of Schnorr signatures for Bitcoin.
items.analogy: Think of the standard plug that makes every device fit.

items.label: x-only public key
items.meaning: A 32-byte key: the x coordinate, with an even y assumed.
items.analogy: Think of a map reference that always faces north.

slides.notes: These cards cover challenge, Fiat-Shamir transform, BIP340 and x-only public key. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: From identity proof to signature
slides.sub: Replace the verifier's challenge by a hash

groups.note: A prover with secret x sends R = kG and receives a challenge e.

rows: chk = lambda t: pm(t) == pa(R, pm(e, X))
groups.note: The response s = k + e x passes; one added to it does not.

rows: sigs = [C.fs_verify(X, m, sig) for m in (b'A', b'B')]
groups.note: Hash the message to get the challenge, and it is a signature.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: proof and signature checks
A signature fits only the message whose hash chose the challenge.

slides.notes: An honest prover's response passes and a wrong one fails. Letting a hash of the message choose the challenge turns the proof into a signature, and the signature fits only that message. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The hash of the message plays the examiner, so no examiner has to be online

slides.title: The signature that was patented for two decades
slides.sub: A patent decided which signature Bitcoin started with

items.cap: Claus-Peter Schnorr, Oberwolfach, 1986 - Konrad Jacobs, MFO, CC BY-SA 2.0 de, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: Claus-Peter Schnorr's signature scheme was patented in the United States as patent 4,995,082, published on 19 February 1991.
WHY: The patent kept the scheme out of open standards, so ECDSA was the only signature Bitcoin knew until 2021.
HOW: The term was the longer of 17 years from grant and 20 from filing, so it ended on 23 February 2010.
SO WHAT: BIP340 is Schnorr's scheme fitted to secp256k1; it went live with taproot, 30 years after the paper.

items.who: Claus-Peter Schnorr, the cryptographer who invented the signature; the company Public Key Partners
items.where: the United States patent office for United States patent 4,995,082, applied for on 23 February 1990 with a priority date of 24 February 1989

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 1991-02-19. Claus-Peter Schnorr published an efficient identification and signature scheme for smart cards in the proceedings of the Crypto '89 conference, and the United States published his patent 4,995,082 on 19 February 1991, filed on 23 February 1990 and claiming priority from 24 February 1989.

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (3 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: linearity
items.meaning: Sums of keys and signatures are keys and signatures of the sum.
items.analogy: Think of adding two bills and paying the total at once.

items.label: batch verification
items.meaning: Many signatures are checked with one combined equation.
items.analogy: Think of weighing a whole crate instead of every apple.

items.label: key prefixing
items.meaning: The public key is hashed into the challenge.
items.analogy: Think of writing your name on your own envelope.

items.label: scriptless multisignature
items.meaning: Keys are added so no script is needed to count signers.
items.analogy: Think of one master key made from several keys.

slides.notes: These cards cover linearity, batch verification, key prefixing and scriptless multisignature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A fixed size: 64 bytes
slides.sub: BIP340 keys are 32 bytes and signatures 64

groups.note: One secret key, one message, and the three objects of BIP340.
For comparison, the compressed key and the ECDSA signature of the same key.
The Schnorr signature verifies, and it has a fixed size.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: bytes per object
The Schnorr signature verifies (yes) and always takes 64 bytes; the x-only key saves one byte over the compressed key.

slides.notes: A BIP340 public key is the x coordinate only, 32 bytes. The signature is 64 bytes, always. The ECDSA signature of the same key is written in DER, whose length varies by a byte or two. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Schnorr is smaller and of fixed size; DER signatures vary

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (4 of 4)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: key cancellation attack
items.meaning: A signer picks a key that cancels the other's key.
items.analogy: Think of a partner who copies your key and subtracts it.

items.label: MuSig2
items.meaning: Key aggregation with hashed weights that defeats the attack.
items.analogy: Think of master keys cut from a mould that includes every member.

items.label: Shamir secret sharing
items.meaning: A secret is the height of a line, shared as points on it.
items.analogy: Think of a treasure map torn so that any two pieces show the way.

items.label: scriptless threshold signature
items.meaning: Any k of n signers produce one signature without a script.
items.analogy: Think of two of three managers opening the vault.

slides.notes: These cards cover key cancellation attack, MuSig2, Shamir secret sharing and scriptless threshold signature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A key that cancels another key
slides.sub: Why adding public keys is not enough

groups.note: Bob waits for Alice's public key, then publishes his own key minus hers.
Against the naive sum of keys, Bob alone makes a valid signature for both.
MuSig2 weights every key by a hash of all keys, and the same attack fails.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the key cancellation attack
After Alice's key is public, Bob picks a key that hides it. Only the weighted aggregate resists.

slides.notes: If keys are simply added, Bob can wait for Alice's key and publish a key that cancels it. Then Bob alone signs for both. With MuSig2's hashed weights the same attack no longer gives Bob's key. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: MuSig2 weights each key by a hash of all keys, which stops the trick

slides.title: Any two of three shares
slides.sub: Shamir's line through points

groups.note: A secret is the height of a line at zero; three shares are points on the line.
Any two points give the line, and with it the secret.
One share alone is consistent with every possible secret.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the secret from the shares
Any two shares give 31337. A single share gives 31414, which is not the secret.

slides.notes: A secret is the height of a line at zero. Each of three shares is a point on that line. Any two points rebuild the line and give the secret, while one share alone fits every possible secret. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Fewer than the threshold reveal nothing; the threshold reveals everything

slides.title: ECDSA signatures
slides.sub: ECDSA is the older seal, with a messier imprint and two valid shapes.

items.meaning: Two formulas, and two valid values of s.
items.analogy: Think of a coin that has two faces and both count.

items.meaning: A signature is written as nested length-prefixed fields.
items.analogy: Think of a parcel with labels on each box inside.

items.meaning: Miners enforce the law; nodes add house rules.
items.analogy: Think of the law of the land and the rules of a shop.

slides.notes: ECDSA signed every Bitcoin payment from 2009 and still signs most. We run its formulas, take apart its byte layout and separate what miners enforce from what nodes prefer.

slides.title: ECDSA signatures: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: ECDSA Signatures
items.meaning: The signature Bitcoin used from 2009; Schnorr joined it in 2021.
items.analogy: Think of the older seal still on every old document.

items.label: ECDSA Algorithm
items.meaning: Sign with a nonce and invert it; verify by rebuilding a point.
items.analogy: Think of a recipe with one step that must be undone exactly.

items.label: Serialization of ECDSA Signatures (DER)
items.meaning: The pair (R, s) written in nested length-prefixed fields.
items.analogy: Think of a nest of labelled boxes inside a parcel.

items.label: ECDSA
items.meaning: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm.

slides.title: ECDSA with the book's formulas
slides.sub: Sign with a chosen nonce, verify by rebuilding a point

groups.note: Sign with an explicit nonce: R is the x coordinate of kG, and s follows.

rows: v = lambda t: C.ecdsa_verify_K(X, h, R, t)
groups.note: Verification rebuilds the point K from s, R and the public key.
Both s and n minus s verify; the low form is the one Bitcoin relays.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the two values of s
Both verify. The smaller one is the low-S form: here it is n - s.

slides.notes: We sign with an explicit nonce and verify by rebuilding the point K. The second valid value of s is n minus s. Nodes relay only the smaller one, the low form. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: If s verifies, so does n minus s: the signature has two forms

items.label: R and s
items.meaning: The two numbers that make up an ECDSA signature.
items.analogy: Think of the two halves of a torn ticket.

items.label: malleability
items.meaning: Anyone can alter a valid signature without the key.
items.analogy: Think of a receipt that can be reprinted in another font.

items.label: DER
items.meaning: Distinguished Encoding Rules, the byte layout of signatures.
items.analogy: Think of the postal rules for addressing a parcel.

items.label: low-S rule
items.meaning: Of s and n minus s, only the smaller is relayed.
items.analogy: Think of of two coin faces, always showing heads.

slides.title: Nine elements in 71 bytes
slides.sub: A DER signature taken apart

groups.note: A real signature plus the one-byte hash type, as it sits in a script.

rows: rows = [(n, len(v) // 2) for n, v in f]
groups.note: The library splits it into the nine elements that the book lists.

rows: total = sum(b for n, b in rows)
groups.note: The elements add up to the length of the whole signature.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: bytes per element (all 71)
R and s take 32 bytes each and the other seven elements one byte each. Strict DER accepts it: yes.

slides.notes: DER writes the signature as nested fields: a type, a length, then R and s, each with its own tag and length, and a final hash-type byte. The byte counts add up to the signature. It is example 13 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Seven of the nine elements are one byte; R and s take 32 each

slides.title: The signature on the page is a real payment
slides.sub: The signature printed in the book is a real payment

items.cap: Bitcoin logo - Grayliptrot, public domain, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: The long hexadecimal signature that the book dissects in its DER section is a real signature from a mined payment.
WHY: A real example can be checked: the chapter recomputes it, and signature, key and transaction agree.
HOW: The payment was mined on 27 December 2013 at 23:11:54 UTC; its R has 33 bytes because its top bit is set.
SO WHAT: Its S is already the low form, so a node would still relay it today.

items.body: Stand-in picture: no picture of the sender exists

items.who: the unnamed sender of a transaction mined in block 277,316 on 27 December 2013; Andreas M. Antonopoulos and David A. Harding
items.where: block 277,316 of the Bitcoin main chain; the signature appears in the DER section of chapter 8 of the 3rd edition

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2013-12-27. The long hexadecimal string that chapter 8 of Mastering Bitcoin uses to explain the DER layout, beginning 3045022100884d142d, is not an invented example: it is the signature in the input of transaction 0627052b6f28912f2703066a912ea577f2ce4da4caa5a5fbd8a57286c345c2f2, mined in block 277,316 at 23:11:54 UTC on 27 December 2013.

slides.title: Valid for miners, refused by nodes
slides.sub: Consensus accepts the high-S twin, policy does not

groups.note: One low-S signature, and the same signature with its high-S twin.

rows: ver = lambda g: L.ecdsa_verify(pk, K.MSG, g)
groups.note: The signature check itself accepts both of the two forms.

rows: verdict = [(ver(g), low(g)) for g in (sig, twin)]
groups.note: The relay rule of low S accepts only one of them.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: consensus against policy
Miners accept both forms. Nodes relay only the low-S form.

slides.notes: Both forms of the signature verify, so a block that contains the high-S twin is valid. A node, however, relays only the low form. Policy is stricter than consensus, and can be changed without a fork. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Policy is a stricter house rule; consensus is the law

slides.title: Policy or consensus?
slides.sub: Why a transaction can be valid and still not be relayed

left.head: Consensus decides what is valid
rows: Every node must agree, or the chain splits.
A change needs a soft or hard fork.
Like the law of the land.

right.head: Policy decides what is relayed
rows: Each node may choose its own rules.
A change needs only a new release.
Like the house rules of a shop.

slides.notes: High S is policy: miners accept it, nodes do not relay it. Strict DER became consensus in 2015. Keeping the two apart explains why a transaction can be valid and yet never reach a miner through ordinary nodes.
slides.take: Policy can change with a release; consensus changes only by a fork

slides.title: Randomness and signature size
slides.sub: The nonce is a one-time pad: use it twice and the secret leaks.

items.meaning: A repeated nonce lets anyone solve for the key.
items.analogy: Think of reusing a one-time pad.

items.meaning: The nonce is derived from key and message.
items.analogy: Think of a recipe that always bakes the same cake.

items.meaning: Signing again until R is small saves a byte.
items.analogy: Think of re-folding a letter until it fits the smaller envelope.

slides.notes: A signature needs a number used once. If it repeats, the key leaks; if it is derived from key and message, it never repeats. The part ends with how it changes the signature size.

slides.title: Randomness and signature size: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: The Importance of Randomness in Signatures
items.meaning: The nonce must be unpredictable and used only once.
items.analogy: Think of a combination lock set by a coin toss, never reused.

items.label: nonce
items.meaning: The one-time secret number k of a signature.
items.analogy: Think of a one-time pad.

items.label: RFC 6979
items.meaning: Derives the nonce from key and message by HMAC.
items.analogy: Think of a recipe that always bakes the same cake.

items.label: nonce reuse
items.meaning: Two signatures with one nonce reveal the private key.
items.analogy: Think of reusing a one-time pad, which hands the secret to a snoop.

slides.notes: These cards cover The Importance of Randomness in Signatures, nonce, RFC 6979 and nonce reuse. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: One nonce, two signatures, no secret
slides.sub: How a reused nonce leaks the key

groups.note: Two different messages signed with the same nonce k.

rows: got, k2 = rec(r, s1, h1, s2, h2)
groups.note: Two equations, two unknowns: subtract, divide, and the key falls out.
With a fresh nonce for the second message, R differs and nothing leaks.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: what two signatures reveal
A single reused nonce hands over the private key; a fresh nonce for the second message does not.

slides.notes: Two signatures with the same nonce give two equations in two unknowns. Subtracting them reveals the nonce and then the private key. A different nonce for the second message leaves nothing to solve. It is example 15 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Android's weak generator made this attack possible in 2013

slides.title: When the phone's random numbers were not random
slides.sub: Weak randomness at signing time gives away the key

items.cap: The Android robot - Google Inc., designed by Irina Blok, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

items: WHAT: On 11 August 2013 Bitcoin.org warned that Android's random number generator was weak and that wallets built on it could be robbed.
WHY: A weak generator can repeat or leak a nonce, and a repeated nonce hands over the private key, as the previous slides computed.
HOW: Alex Klyubin of Google explained the flaw on 14 August; Bitcoin Wallet and other wallets shipped updates.
SO WHAT: RFC 6979 derives the nonce from key and message, which is why Bitcoin Core no longer needs a good generator for it.

items.body: Stand-in: the platform, not the incident

items.who: Alex Klyubin, the Android security engineer who explained the cause; the Bitcoin Wallet, blockchain.info
items.where: Android phones worldwide, and the Bitcoin.org network alert; Android Developers Blog, 14 August 2013

slides.notes: This is a true story, dated 2013-08-11. On 11 August 2013 Bitcoin.org published an alert that the Android component that generates secure random numbers contained critical weaknesses, which made every wallet generated on Android vulnerable to theft, and named Bitcoin Wallet, blockchain.info, BitcoinSpinner and Mycelium Wallet; Bitcoin Wallet 3.15 rotated keys automatically.

slides.title: The nonce derived from the key
slides.sub: RFC 6979 removes the random number

groups.note: Derive the nonce from the secret key and the hash of the message.
The same message gives the same nonce; another message gives another.
So the signature is repeatable too, and no random number is needed.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the derived nonce
Nothing random is drawn, so there is nothing to repeat by accident.

slides.notes: RFC 6979 derives the nonce by keyed hashing of the secret key and the message. It never repeats for different messages, and a signature can be repeated and compared exactly in a test. It is example 16 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Same key and message always give the same nonce, and so the same signature

slides.title: About half are one byte longer
slides.sub: Signature length and the high R

rows: ms = [L.sha256(b'm%d' % i) for i in range(200)]
groups.note: Two hundred different messages, all signed with the same key.

rows: lens = [len(L.ecdsa_sign(K.SK, m)) for m in ms]
groups.note: A 33-byte R, needed when its top bit is set, makes the signature longer.
Count the lengths: about half of all signatures are one byte longer.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: signatures of each length, of 200
Signatures with a 33-byte R are one byte longer. Bitcoin Core signs again until R is small.

slides.notes: When the top bit of R is set, DER adds a zero byte, so the signature has 71 bytes instead of 70. Over 200 signatures about half are longer. Core grinds the nonce to avoid the extra byte. It is example 17 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Bitcoin Core signs again until R is small, to save a byte

slides.title: Segwit signing
slides.sub: Segwit changed what is signed, as a cheque that also states the amount.

items.meaning: The old algorithm re-reads the transaction per input.
items.analogy: Think of reading the whole book again for every page you sign.

items.meaning: New signatures cover the value being spent.
items.analogy: Think of a cheque that states the sum it releases.

items.meaning: A taproot spend carries one 64-byte signature.
items.analogy: Think of a single stamp in place of a pile of papers.

slides.notes: Segregated witness changed what is hashed when a transaction is signed. We count the bytes of the old and the new method and see why the amount is now part of the signature.

slides.title: Segwit signing: key concepts
slides.sub: Each card: the meaning in a few words, then something you already know

items.label: Segregated Witness's New Signing Algorithm
items.meaning: BIP143 hashes less and signs the spent amount.
items.analogy: Think of reading the table of contents instead of the whole book.

items.label: BIP143
items.meaning: The signature hash of segregated witness version 0.
items.analogy: Think of a new form with a box for the sum.

items.label: O(n) hashing
items.meaning: BIP143 hashes a number of bytes in proportion to the inputs.
items.analogy: Think of one walk down the line instead of a full lap per person.

items.label: taproot signature
items.meaning: A BIP340 signature over the BIP341 message, 64 bytes.
items.analogy: Think of one stamp that stands for the whole bundle.

slides.notes: These cards cover Segregated Witness's New Signing Algorithm, BIP143, O(n) hashing and taproot signature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.take: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Quadratic hashing
slides.sub: Old signing against BIP143

groups.note: Transactions of 1, 10, 100 and 1000 inputs.
Count the bytes that enter SHA-256 with the old algorithm and with BIP143.

rows: ratio = [round(a / b, 1) for a, b in zip(old, new)]
groups.note: The old way hashes more and more per input; BIP143 grows in a straight line.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: old bytes hashed divided by BIP143 bytes, by inputs
At 1,000 inputs the old method hashes 41,107,000 bytes and BIP143 254,130: 161.8 times more.

slides.notes: The old algorithm hashes almost the whole transaction again for every input. BIP143 hashes the shared parts once. The ratio of the two grows with the number of inputs. It is example 18 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: Doubling the inputs roughly quadruples the bytes the old method hashes

slides.title: BIP143 signs the amount
slides.sub: A wallet can no longer be lied to about the value

groups.note: One input; the script code of a pay-to-key-hash coin.

rows: v0 = lambda a: L.sighash_v0(sc, tx, 0, 1, a).hex()[:12]
groups.note: Digest of the BIP143 algorithm for an amount of 5000 and for 5001 satoshis.
The old algorithm has no amount in it, so a wallet could be told any value.

items.cap: run under Python 3.14.6 - L, C and K are the chapter library of the page

items.body: Result: the signed digest
The BIP143 digest moves with the amount. The legacy digest has no amount that could move.

slides.notes: In the old algorithm the signer never saw the value of the coin it spent. In BIP143 the amount is part of the digest, so a wrong amount gives a different digest and an invalid signature. It is example 19 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.take: The new digest changes with the amount; the old one cannot

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.sub: One line per part, each provable from its slides

items: A signature is checked from message, public key and signature; scalars wrap at n and the digest is what is signed.
A SIGHASH flag chooses what is signed, and SINGLE with no matching output signs the number one.
Schnorr turns a three-move proof into 64 bytes; keys add up safely only with MuSig2, and shares give thresholds.
ECDSA has two forms of s and a nested byte layout; a reused nonce leaks the key and RFC 6979 prevents it.
Segwit hashes less and signs the amount; policy is stricter than consensus, and standards moved after print.

slides.notes: These five lines are the deck in miniature, one for each group of parts. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all twenty examples.
slides.take: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt
